examples.question: Should Koppert develop a differentiated proposition for home gardeners, building on its biological crop protection for professional growers, or stay with professional growers? What evidence would justify either choice?

theories.T1: Home gardeners will adopt Koppert's biological controls if they perceive them as convenient, easy to use, and safe for children and pets, leading to higher purchase frequency and willingness to pay a premium.
theories.T2: Home gardeners will adopt Koppert's biological controls if they perceive them as a status symbol or a way to differentiate their garden, leading to higher purchase frequency and willingness to pay a premium.

arguments.name: Home-gardener paid pre-order positioning test
arguments.method: Target customers: Dutch home gardeners who bought a garden pest-control product in the last 12 months, recruited online. Treatment: Two arms, same lady beetles and price: (A) a ready-to-use release tube with 'safe for children and pets, open and release' messaging (T1 mechanism); (B) a premium presentation box with 'a garden to be proud of' messaging (T2 mechanism). Control: A plain professional-style sachet with technical instructions only; same lady beetles and same price.
arguments.sample: 900 home gardeners (300 per arm) in the Netherlands, recruited via Dutch gardening Facebook groups and garden-center email newsletters, screened for a garden pest-control purchase in the past 12 months, then randomly assigned.
arguments.measure: Paid pre-order conversion: share of visitors in each arm who complete a €5 deposit toward a spring shipment of a lady-beetle release pack, tracked by unique link.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A (safety/ease) has the highest paid pre-order rate, at least 8 percentage points above control and at least 5 points above arm B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B (premium/status) has the highest paid pre-order rate, at least 8 percentage points above control and at least 5 points above arm A.

arguments.decision_rule: Develop the home proposition only if one arm's paid pre-order rate beats control by at least 8 percentage points AND beats the other arm by at least 5 points; the winning arm sets the positioning. If neither arm beats control by at least 8 points, stay with professional growers. If arm A wins: run a garden-center pilot of a ready-to-use safety/ease line. If arm B wins: run a specialty-retail pilot of a premium presentation line. If neither beats control: stay focused on professional growers and do not build a home line.

justification.learned: Koppert already reaches individual buyers: koppert-lo-canada says Koppert Canada serves "the professional grower and the home gardening enthusiast"; koppert-martha-visit shows a garden visit; koppert-wsu-shipped says lady beetles are "shipped to farmers and home gardeners alike". koppert-about-founded is only a founding story. koppert-agro-ban shows France banning non-agricultural pesticide sales from Jan 2019 (opportunity but regulatory risk). None quantify home-gardener demand, willingness to pay, or adoption; demand is unknown. The "supports" ratings for T1/T2 reflect existence/capability, not proven demand.
justification.uncertain: Whether measurable home-gardener demand exists; no source shows purchases, repeat use, or willingness to pay. Which mechanism drives buying: T1 (safety/convenience) or T2 (status/premium). Whether biological controls for amateurs are legally sellable in the EU after France's 2019 non-agricultural pesticide ban, and whether live-organism products can be profitably shipped to consumers. Sources predate 2026, so current demand is unverified.
justification.why_next: The decision depends on observable demand, which the dossier does not establish. A paid pre-order test separates T1 from T2 because each predicts its own positioning variant wins on real deposits, and it separates expansion from staying if neither variant beats the neutral control. I rely on T1 and T2 and on koppert-lo-canada (capability to reach enthusiasts) and koppert-agro-ban (regulatory context).

examples.question: It is March 2016. Should Embrace Innovations develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its infant-warming technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Parents of low‑birth‑weight infants will adopt a home‑use infant warmer if they perceive it as a medical necessity that reduces the risk of SIDS and is affordable, because they are willing to pay a premium for a product that addresses a serious health concern.
theories.T2: Parents of low‑birth‑weight infants will adopt a home‑use infant warmer if they perceive it as a convenient, affordable way to monitor their baby’s temperature and health at home, because they value time‑saving and ease of use, and are willing to pay a price that reflects the convenience.

arguments.name: Deposit test of medical-necessity vs convenience home warmer propositions
arguments.method: Target customers: US parents of premature or low-birth-weight infants who have brought, or are about to bring, their baby home, screened by a short questionnaire. Treatment: Landing page A (T1): home warming kit positioned as a clinical-grade safety device, 'developed from neonatal-care technology to help keep premature and low-birth-weight babies at a stable, safe temperature at home', with medical validation and a high/low temperature alarm; price $129 with a 'Reserve with a $20 refundable deposit' call-to-action. Control: Landing page B (T2): same layout, same $129 price and same $20 refundable deposit call-to-action, but positioned as a convenience device, 'easy at-home temperature monitoring and warming, fewer middle-of-the-night worries and fewer trips back to the clinic', with auto-regulating warmth, one-button use and smartphone temperature tracking.
arguments.sample: About 600 screened parents (300 per arm, proposed), recruited over 4 weeks via paid social ads and posts in US preemie-parent and NICU support groups, then randomly assigned to one landing page; no claim of statistical power is made.
arguments.measure: Proportion of visitors in each arm who complete the $20 refundable deposit within 6 weeks of the landing page going live. This is a real, if modest, financial commitment; it establishes relative interest in each proposition but not final full-price purchase.

prediction_by_theory.T1: The medical-necessity arm yields a higher deposit rate than the convenience arm, because parents of low-birth-weight infants act on health-risk fear and commit to the safety-focused device.
prediction_by_theory.T2: The convenience arm yields a higher deposit rate than the medical arm, because these parents value time-saving and easy monitoring and commit to the convenient device.

arguments.decision_rule: Proceed if one arm's deposit rate is at least 4% and at least 1.5 times the other arm's rate. Stop if both arms' deposit rates are below 2%. Treat 2% to 4%, or a margin under 1.5x, as inconclusive and run a small qualitative follow-up with depositors. If the medical arm wins, run a bounded paid pilot (proposed ~100-unit prototype run) through a pharmacy or medical channel, contingent on legal review of health claims. If the convenience arm wins, run the same-sized pilot through baby-retail or D2C. If both arms are below 2%, stop the home-kit consumer proposition and keep the current B2B focus and existing Little Lotus line. If inconclusive, interview depositors before committing further.

justification.learned: Public sources show Embrace began as a clinical warmer for low-resource settings (embrace-ee-origin) and launched in India in 2011 for institutional use (embrace-smg-launch). By Feb 2016 it sells consumer Little Lotus swaddles at $85 after a cut from $98 (embrace-cnbc-price): this proves a consumer channel and price point, not demand for a home medical warmer. T1 rests only on a company assertion about SIDS risk (embrace-her-sids). T2 has no direct support; embrace-ee-origin is neutral on convenience. A 2012 GSB case notes investor pressure against small segments (embrace-gsb-investors). No source shows revenue, unit sales or independent demand; home-warmer demand is unknown.
justification.uncertain: Whether parents of premature or low-birth-weight infants will pay for a home warming kit, and whether medical necessity (T1) or convenience (T2) drives commitment. Whether Embrace can legally market the SIDS claim on which T1 rests (embrace-her-sids). Whether the home LBW segment is large enough for investor returns (embrace-gsb-investors). Whether a $20 deposit predicts full-price purchase, and whether preemie/NICU recruitment oversamples engaged parents.
justification.why_next: The test separates T1 from T2 because both arms show the same $129 product and deposit call-to-action but activate different causal drivers: T1 predicts the medical-necessity/safety arm yields more deposits (health-risk fear), while T2 predicts the convenience/monitoring arm yields more (time-saving value). Holding price and presentation otherwise equal, a difference in deposit rate isolates which motivation drives real commitment. The threshold also acts as a go/no-go gate: near-zero deposits in both arms imply no consumer demand for the kit, supporting staying B2B or stopping.

examples.question: Should Superior Glove develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing work-glove offering? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will purchase Superior Glove gloves if they perceive them as a premium, high‑performance product for specific, high‑risk activities (e.g., outdoor recreation, cycling, gardening) because they trust the brand’s reputation for cut‑resistant materials and safety.
theories.T2: Consumers will purchase Superior Glove gloves if they perceive them as a safety‑first product recommended by trusted professionals (e.g., OSHA inspectors, safety managers) because they trust the brand’s safety credentials and want to meet regulatory requirements.

arguments.name: Paid-deposit landing page test of a consumer glove proposition
arguments.method: Target customers: US adults aged 25-60 with interests in gardening, DIY and outdoor recreation, reached via paid Meta ads. Treatment: Two treatment landing pages, both offering the same first-run consumer glove at $24.99 with a $5 refundable pre-order deposit, same photo and page format. Arm A (T1): premium activity-specific positioning - 'Kevlar/Dyneema cut-resistant performance, engineered for serious gardeners'. Arm B (T2): safety-first positioning - 'ANSI A4 cut-rated; the glove safety professionals recommend for home use'. Control: A third landing page offering the identical glove at the same $24.99 price and $5 deposit, described only as a generic 'cut-resistant work glove' with no consumer use-case or safety-endorsement positioning.
arguments.sample: Paid Meta ads randomized 1:1:1 to the three pages, about 1,500 unique visitors per arm (4,500 total), recruited over four weeks.
arguments.measure: Primary: deposit conversion rate, the share of unique visitors who complete the $5 refundable pre-order deposit. Committing at the premium $24.99 price also signals willingness to pay that price.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A (premium activity-specific) will have the highest deposit conversion rate, beating the control by at least 8 percentage points and beating Arm B by at least 5 points.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B (safety-endorsed) will have the highest deposit conversion rate, beating the control by at least 8 percentage points and beating Arm A by at least 5 points.

arguments.decision_rule: Proceed only if the winning arm's deposit rate is at least 5% AND at least 8 percentage points above the control AND at least 5 points above the other treatment; otherwise no consumer expansion. Arm A wins: run a small production and retail/distributor pilot of a premium activity-specific glove. Arm B wins: pilot a safety-positioned consumer glove with professional-endorsement messaging. Control wins or neither treatment clears 5%: do not invest in a consumer proposition and keep the B2B work-glove focus.

justification.learned: The three sources show capability and channel, not demand: superior-cut-specialist claims cut-resistant gloves and Kevlar®/Dyneema® licensing; superior-distribution-only says sales went to "distribution only"; superior-nc-plant confirms a 2025 US PPE plant. Searches for Amazon, an online store and consumer reviews found nothing, so reach to individual buyers and demand are unknown. T1 (premium activity-specific) and T2 (safety-endorsed) remain open hypotheses with capability or neutral evidence, not customer behaviour.
justification.uncertain: Demand is unknown: no source shows consumers buy or search for Superior Glove outside work channels. The test measures paid deposits for a simulated offer, but distribution-only sales means it cannot show a route to individual buyers exists or that deposits become shipped sales. Deposits are commitment, not full purchases. Sample sizes, thresholds, cost and duration are proposed analyst parameters, not market facts.
justification.why_next: A test is justified because T1 and T2 make different predictions under the same offer: T1 predicts the premium activity-specific arm converts more, T2 predicts the safety-endorsed arm converts more, and both are checked against a generic control representing no differentiation. A winning differentiated arm with a real $5 deposit would justify a small pilot; a control win or no clear winner would stop the consumer investment. This separates T1 from T2 on mechanism (performance trust versus professional safety endorsement), using a real-money deposit at a premium price rather than stated preference.

arguments.name: Paid pre-order test: eco water-saving vs pre-assembled convenience drip kit
arguments.method: Target customers: Home and balcony/terrace gardeners in a water-stressed Indian city (e.g., Bengaluru), where Netafim already sells consumer kits; screened online to own or plan a garden/terrace and be in-market for irrigation within the next 6 months. Treatment: Two arms shown an identical Netafim-branded garden-kit page with the same premium price and layout. Arm A kit includes a flow regulator/water meter and eco-certification and arrives unassembled (eco attribute). Arm B kit arrives pre-assembled, plug-and-play, low-maintenance, with no eco extras (convenience attribute). Control: Unbranded generic drip kit, unassembled, no eco extras, priced about 30% below the Netafim arms, with the same page layout.
arguments.sample: Recruit 300 eligible gardeners via Facebook/Instagram ads and a local panel, randomly assigned 100 per arm; pay €20 incentive each, and offer a refundable €15 deposit to reserve the kit at launch.
arguments.measure: Primary: share of each arm placing the refundable €15 pre-order deposit. Secondary: self-reported top purchase reason and willingness-to-pay ceiling recorded after the deposit decision.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Deposit rate in Arm A (eco) exceeds Arm B (convenience) by at least 10 percentage points, and A beats control; water conservation is the top stated reason among A buyers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Deposit rate in Arm B (convenience) exceeds Arm A (eco) by at least 10 percentage points, and B beats control; convenience/low-maintenance is the top stated reason among B buyers.

arguments.decision_rule: Decision rule: ≥10 percentage-point deposit-rate advantage of one arm over the other, and that arm must beat control by ≥10 points. If A−B ≥10pp and A−control ≥10pp, eco-led proposition; if B−A ≥10pp and B−control ≥10pp, convenience-led; otherwise no differentiated consumer investment. If A wins, pilot an eco-certified water-saving kit for home gardeners and test sell-through with one retail/online partner. If B wins, pilot a pre-assembled plug-and-play kit for balcony/terrace users. If neither beats control, stop consumer expansion and stay with B2B/current lines.

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated Bubble Wrap proposition for home moving because they value the sound and tactile experience of popping the wrap, and they seek a fun, stress‑reducing activity for moving tasks.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated Bubble Wrap proposition for small‑business packaging because they need lightweight, space‑saving protective material that reduces shipping costs and improves storage efficiency.

arguments.name: Poppable vs pop-less pre-order test across home movers and small shippers
arguments.method: Target customers: US adults in two groups: (a) 300 people who moved in the past 12 months or plan to move within 12 weeks; (b) 300 small e-commerce sellers shipping at least 5 orders per week. Treatment: A branded Bubble Wrap landing page offering the original poppable wrap, described factually as 'pops when pressed,' at $14.99 with a $5 non-refundable pre-order deposit. Control: The identical branded Bubble Wrap landing page offering the pop-less wrap, described factually as 'takes up 1/50th the space, does not pop,' at the same $14.99 with the same $5 non-refundable deposit; layout, brand and price are otherwise identical.
arguments.sample: Recruited via paid Facebook and Instagram ads with a two-question screener; 300 qualifying people per segment are randomly assigned 50/50 to the poppable or pop-less page.
arguments.measure: Completed $5 non-refundable pre-order deposit (applied to the $14.99 price), reported as the deposit conversion rate in each of the four cells (segment x poppable/pop-less).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Home movers shown the poppable page convert at 12% or more and at least 5 points above the pop-less page; small shippers show no 5-point pop-less advantage because the fun/stress mechanism does not motivate them.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Small shippers shown the pop-less page convert at 12% or more and at least 5 points above the poppable page; home movers show no 5-point poppable advantage because the efficiency mechanism does not motivate them.

arguments.decision_rule: Favour T1 if home-mover poppable conversion is 12% or more and exceeds home-mover pop-less by at least 5 points, while shipper pop-less does not beat shipper poppable by 5 points. Favour T2 if shipper pop-less conversion is 12% or more and exceeds shipper poppable by at least 5 points, while home-mover poppable does not beat home-mover pop-less by 5 points. Otherwise stop. If T1 is favoured, run a limited pilot of the poppable moving kit through a consumer marketplace or retail listing before scaling. If T2 is favoured, run a small-business pilot of the space-saver kit with an e-commerce platform or office-supply retailer. If neither threshold is met, recommend no consumer expansion and refocus on the B2B core.

justification.learned: Bubble Wrap's appeal is the popping sensation, a "stress reducer disguised as package cushioning" (sealedair-ap-stress); losing poppability caused public anger (sealedair-cbc-anger). The pop-less redesign targets online retailers as it takes up one-fiftieth the space (sealedair-fortune-ecom), yet Sealed Air's best seller is liquid foam, not Bubble Wrap (sealedair-dz-foam). Bubble Wrap was 3.6% of sales in 2012, down from 5.7% in 2010, and Sealed Air considered eliminating it (sealedair-cbc-share; sealedair-sbt-eliminate). Stated end markets are B2B (sealedair-pr-markets). No source shows consumer willingness to pay, purchase behaviour, or current consumer reach, so demand is unproven.
justification.uncertain: Whether pop appeal converts into paid demand for home-moving (T1) and whether small shippers will pay for the pop-less space-saver (T2) are both unknown. The test cannot fully separate the physical attribute from its factual description, and ad-recruited respondents may differ from the broader market; a pre-order shows willingness to commit, not repeat or scaled demand. Sealed Air's consumer retail channel and group-level-only financials remain unknown.
justification.why_next: A test is worth its cost because the separating question is real purchasing behaviour, which none of the sources answer. It separates T1 from T2 because T1's fun/stress mechanism (sealedair-ap-stress) predicts home movers commit to the poppable wrap, while T2's efficiency mechanism (sealedair-fortune-ecom) predicts small shippers commit to the pop-less wrap. arguments.name: Plant-health vs convenience deposit test for Netafim garden kits
arguments.method: Target customers: Urban home gardeners in India who own a balcony, terrace, small plot, pots or grow bags and are in the market for irrigation; Netafim already sells NetBow and ArrowFlow garden kits in this market. arguments.sample: Recruit 800 people via paid Facebook and Instagram ads geo-targeted to Indian metros using neutral creative that mentions neither plant health nor convenience; randomise click-throughs 1:1 to the two pages, 400 per arm.
arguments.measure: The share of each arm that completes the refundable ₹499 deposit for a pre-order, a real purchase commitment rather than stated intent; also record the stated reason at checkout as a secondary check.

examples.question: It is early 2011. Should MSA (Mine Safety Appliances) develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its respirators, hard hats and fall-protection products? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt MSA safety products for DIY and outdoor recreation if they perceive the products as reliable, brand trusted, and convenient to purchase through retail channels.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt MSA safety products for DIY and outdoor recreation if they perceive the products as a status symbol or brand prestige, leading them to purchase multiple pairs for different activities.

arguments.reason: No experiment can change the decision. T1 (trust) and T2 (prestige) both predict premium DIY/outdoor purchases and both imply investing, differing only on driver and premium (10% vs 15%); a test is thus a trust-vs-prestige messaging test, not go/no-go. The real question — independent premium demand — lacks a rival theory and needs company sell-through/deposit data beyond €20,000/12 weeks.

justification.learned: MSA has had a consumer arm since 1998 (msa-jv-1998). Company statements say by 2011 it sold through home-center/hardware/rental channels incl. The Home Depot, Do it Best, True Value (msa-jv-retailers), in 10,000+ storefronts, used by 'millions of North American consumers' (msa-jv-storefronts). These are company assertions about reach, not independent demand or willingness-to-pay evidence. msa-jchs-diy shows DIY ≈18% of 2011 US improvement spending, 29% among under-35s, but nothing on safety gear. Both that Dec-2012 post and the Jul-2011 JV release post-date early 2011, so decision-date demand evidence was only MSA's own statements.
justification.uncertain: Whether DIY/outdoor consumers would actually pay a premium for MSA-branded safety gear is unknown: no source independently measures demand, willingness to pay, or repeat purchase. Both T1 and T2 assume premium demand and differ only in driver (trust vs prestige) and premium size (10% vs 15%), so it is also uncertain whether that driver difference matters for go/no-go. Financials and MSA's internal sell-through data are not in the dossier.
justification.why_next: Declining is right. T1 and T2 do not separate on the decision: both predict DIY/outdoor consumers will buy at a premium, differing only in driver and premium size (10% vs 15%), so a test distinguishing them is messaging, not go/no-go, and the real uncertainty — independent premium demand — is not represented by a rival theory. examples.question: Should Koppert develop a differentiated proposition for home gardeners, building on its biological crop protection for professional growers, or stay with professional growers? What evidence would justify either choice?

theories.T1: Home gardeners will adopt Koppert's biological controls if they perceive them as convenient, safe, and effective, leading to repeat purchases and brand loyalty.
theories.T2: Home gardeners will adopt Koppert's biological controls if they perceive them as a status symbol or a reflection of environmental values, leading to higher purchase frequency and brand loyalty.

arguments.name: Deposit test: convenience/safety vs eco-status framing for a Koppert garden kit
arguments.method: Target customers: Dutch home gardeners aged 25-65 who own a garden and report pest damage on edible or ornamental plants in the past 12 months, recruited via Facebook/Instagram ads and Dutch gardening-community newsletters. Treatment: A proposed 'Koppert Garden Beneficials Starter Kit' (predatory mites for aphids and spider mites, €39.99) shown with convenience/safety framing: easy single-release sachets, no chemical residues, and clear effectiveness steps, with a call-to-action to pay a €10 deposit to pre-order, refunded if Koppert does not launch. Control: The identical kit, price, channel and €10 deposit call-to-action, but presented only with eco-status framing: 'the choice of conscious gardeners', sustainability and prestige imagery, membership-style language.
arguments.sample: Recruit 600 gardeners (300 per arm) over 12 weeks through targeted social ads with a short screener (garden ownership, pest problem in the last 12 months, interest in non-chemical control); randomly assign eligible visitors to the two landing pages.
arguments.measure: Share of each arm's eligible visitors who pay the €10 deposit (deposits / unique visitors). This is a real commitment rather than stated intent, but it measures initial willingness to pay, not repeat purchase or full-price conversion.

prediction_by_theory.T1: The convenience/safety arm will have a deposit rate at least 5 percentage points higher than the eco-status arm, because reduced perceived effort and risk, not status, is what makes risk-averse gardeners commit.
prediction_by_theory.T2: The eco-status arm will have a deposit rate at least 5 percentage points higher than the convenience/safety arm, because eco-conscious, status-motivated gardeners commit when the offer signals prestige rather than mere convenience.

arguments.decision_rule: Enter the home-gardener market only if the winning arm's deposit rate is at least 8% (proposed). If both arms are below 8%, stay with professional growers. If both clear 8% and differ by less than 5 percentage points, framing is not decisive and the lower-cost convenience/safety version should be piloted. Winning arm at or above 8%: run a 6-month, one-region retail/DTC pilot of that framing with a small kit production run. Both arms below 8%: stop home-gardener work and stay with professional growers. Both at or above 8% but within 5 points: pilot the cheaper convenience/safety version.

justification.learned: Evidence is thin: it shows reach, not demand. koppert-lo-canada (2007) says Koppert Canada supplied 'both the professional grower and the home gardening enthusiast' - capability, not purchase data. koppert-martha-visit (2018) is one affluent consumer's advisory visit, not scalable demand. koppert-wsu-shipped (2017) says lady beetles are 'shipped to farmers and home gardeners alike' - some buy, but not at Koppert's premium. koppert-agro-ban (2017) shows France banning non-agricultural pesticide sales to amateurs from Jan 2019 - a possible tailwind, unclear for biologicals. No source gives demand, adoption, or willingness to pay.
justification.uncertain: Open: whether enough home gardeners will pay a premium for a differentiated Koppert retail offer, and whether the driver is convenience/safety (T1) or eco-status (T2). A €10 deposit is real but partial - initial willingness to pay, not repeat or full-price conversion. Two arms lack a neutral arm, so intrinsic vs framing demand is not fully separable, though the absolute bar still decides go/no-go. A positive result still needs production and channel work.
justification.why_next: A test is worth running because a result can change the decision: the absolute threshold decides enter vs stay with professional growers, and the arm comparison separates T1 from T2 (each predicts its own framing wins by at least 5 percentage points because each names a different purchase driver - reduced effort/risk vs status/eco-signalling). koppert-lo-canada and koppert-wsu-shipped establish feasibility/reach but not demand, so a cheap real-commitment deposit test is the next justified step before any production or channel investment.

examples.question: It is mid-2014. Should ResMed develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its non-contact sleep-sensing technology and sleep-medicine expertise? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Individuals with sleep apnoea will adopt a home sleep test device if they perceive it as convenient and accurate, and if they are willing to pay a premium for non-contact technology that avoids the need for clinic visits.
theories.T2: Insurance companies will cover home sleep tests if they are validated against polysomnography and demonstrate clinical efficacy, leading consumers to adopt home testing because they avoid clinic visits and reduce out-of-pocket costs.

arguments.name: Deposit-reservation test of a non-contact home sleep monitor: out-of-pocket vs insurance-covered
arguments.method: Target customers: US adults aged 30-65 with suspected or diagnosed sleep apnoea or a referral for a sleep study, excluding anyone who completed a sleep study in the last 12 months. Treatment: A product page for the non-contact sleep monitor ('validated against polysomnography', 'no clinic visit', 'measures sleep and breathing') priced at $149.99, with a call-to-action requiring a $25 fully refundable deposit to reserve the device at that out-of-pocket price. Control: The identical product page and description, but priced at '$0 with insurance coverage'; it requires the same $25 fully refundable deposit, returned once the buyer's insurance coverage is verified.
arguments.sample: Recruit 800 US adults via paid search and social ads targeting sleep-apnoea terms and communities over 8 weeks; randomly assign 400 to each offer. Ad spend, landing page and deposit processing sit within the €20,000 budget; deposits are refunded.
arguments.measure: The share of visitors in each arm who complete the $25 refundable deposit within 14 days of first landing (a real commitment rather than stated purchase intent).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 8% of the out-of-pocket arm completes the deposit, and the covered arm is not more than about double that rate, because patients who value convenience and accuracy will pay the $149.99 premium out-of-pocket.
prediction_by_theory.T2: The out-of-pocket arm completes below 4% (willingness to pay under $100) while the covered arm completes at least 15%, because only insurance coverage removes the financial barrier and drives commitment.

arguments.decision_rule: Proceed to a bounded direct-to-consumer pilot if the out-of-pocket arm is at or above 8%; shift to a payer-covered/B2B route if the out-of-pocket arm is below 8% and the covered arm is at or above 15%; stop (no expansion) if the out-of-pocket arm is below 8% and the covered arm is below 15%. If T1 is supported (out-of-pocket ≥8%), run a small direct-to-consumer pilot with a limited production run and one retail or direct channel. If T2 is supported (covered ≥15% and out-of-pocket <8%), pursue home healthcare dealers and payers for a covered home-test route rather than a premium consumer product. If neither threshold is met, recommend no expansion and revisit only after improving accuracy or the channel.

justification.learned: As of mid-2014 ResMed's 10-K shows it sells via sleep clinics and home healthcare dealers, who then sell to the patient (resmed-10k-clinics, resmed-10k-dealer); its route to individuals is indirect. The 2011 BiancaMed deal supplied the non-contact SleepMinder (resmed-pr-biancamed), but 2011 validation showed 78% accuracy and kappa 0.38, worse in high-AHI (resmed-pm-dechazal2011). No source shows consumer demand, willingness to pay, or insurance coverage. The $149.99 S+ price is October 2014, after the decision date, so unusable. T1 and T2 rest on thin company assertions; demand is unknown.
justification.uncertain: The decisive unknowns are whether individuals with sleep apnoea would actually pay out-of-pocket (T1) or would commit only when insurance covers the device (T2), and whether ResMed can reach individual buyers directly rather than through dealers. The non-contact sensor's modest diagnostic agreement (kappa 0.38) also leaves open whether the proposition can be a credible home test or must be positioned as wellness monitoring. theories.T1: Parents of premature and low-birth-weight infants in low-resource settings will adopt a home infant warmer if it is priced below $100 and marketed as a life-saving medical device that reduces the risk of SIDS.

arguments.name: Pre-order test of medical vs premium consumer warmer positioning
arguments.method: Target customers: Expectant parents and parents of infants under six months in urban India (Bengaluru, Mumbai) who shop baby products online. Chosen because the Embrace Nest is widely used in India (embrace-smg-launch) and the company already sells online (embrace-cnbc-price). Treatment: Same product (Little Lotus-style warming swaddle) presented as a premium status item: 'NASA-inspired, design-led essential for modern families,' priced at $120 (about Rs 7,800), sold on a branded landing page with a refundable Rs 500 deposit. Control: Identical product presented as a medical device: 'clinically-inspired temperature regulation for premature and low-birth-weight babies; helps avoid temperature-linked SIDS,' priced at $85 (about Rs 5,500), same landing-page layout and deposit.
arguments.sample: Identical Facebook/Instagram ads to matched urban-India parent audiences, randomly split 50/50 to the two pages. Target 1,000 visitors per arm (2,000 total) over 8-10 weeks; exclude anyone who saw both pages.
arguments.measure: Share of visitors who complete a pre-order and pay a refundable Rs 500 (about $8) deposit within seven days. A paid deposit is real commitment, not stated intent.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Medical arm (control, $85) deposit conversion at least 8% and at least 4 percentage points above the premium arm (premium at most 4%), because price-sensitive parents with a medical need respond to safety framing and a low price.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Premium arm (treatment, $120) deposit conversion at least 6% and at least equal to the medical arm, because status-seeking parents prefer premium price and design framing and are not driven by discount medical messaging.

arguments.decision_rule: Proceed with the medical proposition if control conversion is at least 8% and control minus treatment is at least 4 points. Proceed with the premium proposition if treatment conversion is at least 6% and treatment is at least equal to control. If both arms are below 5%, do not invest in a consumer proposition. Bundled price and positioning means a win shows the whole proposition, not price alone. Medical win: build a small prototype run and a hospital-partner pilot. Premium win: keep the existing Little Lotus direction and extend it to the use case through current online retail. Both below 5%: stop the consumer proposition and remain B2B. A follow-up 2x2 price/positioning test can isolate price if the win is close.

justification.learned: Public sources show Embrace began as a Stanford design challenge for premature and low-birth-weight infants in settings without reliable incubators (embrace-ee-origin, company assertion). A consumer product exists: Little Lotus swaddles sell on the company website, cut from $98 to $85 (embrace-cnbc-price). Embrace claims it may even reduce the risk of SIDS (embrace-her-sids, company assertion). No source shows actual individual purchases or demand for a home-warming product.
justification.uncertain: Whether individual buyers would pay for a consumer home-warming proposition and why is unknown: T1 (medical need, under $100) vs T2 (premium status). T2's status mechanism has no direct evidence; embrace-cnbc-price shows a premium product online, not status buying. Legal ability to make medical/SIDS claims for home use is unknown; no financial data available. No evidence shows purchase behaviour, so neither theory is supported by observed demand.
justification.why_next: A pre-order test separates T1 from T2 because each theory predicts a different bundle wins under real commitment: T1 predicts the $85 medical arm converts higher, T2 predicts the $120 premium arm converts higher. A "both fail" result points to no consumer extension, which changes the decision across all four open alternatives. It relies on T1, T2, the observed premium online channel (embrace-cnbc-price) and the India market presence (embrace-smg-launch).

examples.question: Should Cotral Lab develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing hearing-protection offering? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Professional musicians will adopt custom-moulded hearing protection if it is marketed as a performanceenhancing tool that preserves sound quality while blocking noise, because they value accurate sound and are willing to pay a premium for a product that does not compromise their craft.
theories.T2: Sleep aid users will adopt custom-moulded hearing protection if it is marketed as a medical-grade solution that reduces sleep disruption caused by background noise, because they seek a product that addresses a specific health concern and are willing to pay for a solution that improves sleep quality.

arguments.name: Deposit test: musician vs sleep-use custom earplugs
arguments.method: Target customers: Arm A: amateur and semi-professional musicians in France who perform or rehearse at least monthly. Arm B: adults in France who report frequent sleep disruption from partner snoring or neighbourhood noise. Both currently use or have tried earplugs. Treatment: Segment-matched differentiated landing page with a non-refundable €50 deposit offer: musicians see performance-enhancing custom earplugs that preserve sound quality while cutting harmful levels; sleep users see medical-grade custom sleep earplugs to reduce noise-driven sleep disruption. Control: The same landing page and the same €50 deposit offer with the current generic positioning, custom-moulded hearing protection for noise, shown to both segments.
arguments.sample: Paid Facebook/Instagram ads in France target the two segments, with a 3-question screener to qualify them. 800 qualified respondents (400 musicians, 400 sleep users) are randomised 50/50 within each segment to treatment vs control.
arguments.measure: Share of qualified visitors who complete a non-refundable €50 deposit toward the custom earplug (applied to the ~€180 price, refundable only if Cotral cannot schedule an impression) within 4 weeks.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Musicians shown the performance-enhancing positioning will deposit at a higher rate (≥8%) than their generic control (≤4%) and than sleep users shown the sleep positioning.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Sleep users shown the medical-grade sleep positioning will deposit at a higher rate (≥8%) than their generic control (≤4%) and than musicians shown the musician positioning.

arguments.decision_rule: Proceed with a segment only if its treatment arm deposits ≥8% AND beats its own control by ≥4 percentage points AND beats the rival segment's treatment arm by ≥4 points. If neither treatment arm reaches 8%, no expansion. Musician arm wins: pilot 30-50 musicians through an audiologist partner to validate full-price purchase and impression logistics. Sleep arm wins: same pilot for sleep users. Neither clears: do not build a consumer proposition; stay with B2B and revisit only if a consumer channel is found.

justification.learned: Cotral Lab is the world's No.1 custom-moulded hearing-protection maker (ctl-deal), uses 3D printing (ctl-3d), in-house filters (ctl-filter), on-site impressions (ctl-onsite), Bluetooth plugs (ctl-it1). Distribution is "primarily through direct channels to end-user companies" (ctl-channel); acquired by Groupe RG (ctl-deal), so individual-buyer reach looks B2B. bockstael-2015-looks found musician appreciation "mainly depended on comfort and looks, while differences in sound quality were less noticeable", undercutting T1. Minuendo sells adjustable musician earplugs (minuendo-claim). T1 and T2 rest on capability claims; no source shows an individual paid or committed.
justification.uncertain: Whether individual buyers would pay a premium or put down a deposit is unknown — no demand evidence found. T1 is weakened because bockstael-2015-looks suggests musicians prioritise comfort and looks over sound quality. T2 has no independent demand evidence. Also unclear whether Cotral's on-site B2B impression model suits individual consumers, and whether a €50 deposit on a ~€180 product clears the hurdle.
justification.why_next: A deposit-backed experiment is the cheapest way to learn whether a differentiated consumer proposition would pull real commitment, which no source shows. It separates T1 from T2 (and both from no expansion) because each theory predicts its own segment will place more non-refundable deposits on the differentiated offer than on the generic control and than the rival segment, so the winning segment plus the treatment-vs-control gap jointly decide whether and where to invest.

examples.question: It is 1946. Should Reynolds Metals develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its aluminium foil rolling capacity? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt Reynolds aluminum foil for home cooking if they perceive it as a convenient, hygienic, and cost-effective alternative to paper or other foil, and if the company provides clear instructions and marketing that highlight its safety and durability.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt Reynolds aluminum foil for outdoor activities (camping, hiking) if they perceive it as lightweight, durable, and safe for food storage, and if the company markets it as a reliable outdoor essential.

arguments.name: Mail-order use-case framing test: kitchen vs outdoor Reynolds Wrap
arguments.method: Target customers: US households that cook or camp, reached by direct mail in 1946. Treatment: A 25-foot roll of Reynolds Wrap offered by mail packaged as 'Reynolds Wrap for the Kitchen,' with a recipe and food-storage instruction card, priced at $0.25 (1946 dollars) with a prepaid order form. Control: The identical 25-foot roll packaged as 'Reynolds Wrap for Camp and Trail,' with outdoor cooking and food-storage instructions, same $0.25 price and same prepaid order form.
arguments.sample: Mail identical offers to 4,000 US households total, 2,000 per version, drawn from one rented, regionally balanced household list and randomized between the two versions so both use cases are tested on the same population.
arguments.measure: Actual paid mail orders returned with payment per arm over 8 weeks, measured as the percentage of each 2,000-household arm that orders.

prediction_by_theory.T1: The kitchen-framed roll produces a higher paid-order rate than the outdoor-framed roll (e.g., 4% vs under 3%), because kitchen hygiene and convenience are the stronger purchase drivers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: The outdoor-framed roll produces a higher paid-order rate than the kitchen-framed roll (e.g., 4% vs under 3%), because lightweight, durable field food storage is the stronger purchase driver.

arguments.decision_rule: Pursue the kitchen proposition (T1) if the kitchen order rate is at least 3% and exceeds the outdoor rate by at least 1 percentage point. Pursue the outdoor proposition (T2) if the outdoor rate is at least 3% and exceeds the kitchen rate by at least 1 percentage point. Otherwise, do not expand to a differentiated consumer line. If T1 wins, run a paid regional grocery pilot of the kitchen foil. If T2 wins, run a small outdoor-retailer pilot. If neither clears the bar, stop consumer differentiation and continue existing B2B and generic foil sales.

justification.learned: Sources show Reynolds had foil-rolling and printed-packaging capability sold to B2B food/cigarette/candy makers (reynolds-lem-packaging), doubled capacity in 1946 by leasing/purchasing six government plants (reynolds-fu-plants), and shifted toward consumer goods after WWII (reynolds-fu-postwar). examples.question: Should Technogym develop a differentiated proposition for home users, beyond its existing premium home equipment and apps, or keep its current consumer offer? What evidence would justify either choice?

theories.T1: Home users will adopt a differentiated proposition if they perceive it as a premium lifestyle experience rather than just a functional product.
theories.T2: Home users will adopt a differentiated proposition if they experience a measurable health benefit that cannot be achieved with generic equipment, such as data-driven coaching or personalized feedback.

arguments.name: Home proposition deposit test: lifestyle vs health framing vs current offer
arguments.method: Target customers: 1,500 adults aged 30-60 in Italy and the UK with household income above 80,000 euros, actively considering a home gym purchase above 2,000 euros in the next six months and not already owning Technogym equipment. Treatment: Two concept landing pages for a new differentiated home proposition, identical in product photos, specs and price, each offering a 99 euro refundable reservation; the Lifestyle variant leads with Italian design, interior-designer consultation and status, while the Health variant leads with data-driven coaching and measurable health outcomes. Control: A landing page for Technogym's current premium home equipment offer, with functional equipment-led copy, the same product specs and price, and the same 99 euro refundable reservation.
arguments.sample: Recruit via paid Meta/Instagram ads and fitness-community posts targeting the profile above; randomly assign 500 visitors per arm to one of the three pages, with the page copy as the only visible difference.
arguments.measure: Primary: share of visitors who complete the 99 euro refundable reservation within 14 days (a real commitment, though weaker than an actual purchase). Secondary: maximum price each visitor states they would pay after viewing the page.

prediction_by_theory.T1: The Lifestyle variant has the highest reservation rate and beats the control by at least 3 percentage points, while the Health variant is no better than the control, because status and design drive the premium purchase.
prediction_by_theory.T2: The Health variant has the highest reservation rate and beats the control by at least 3 percentage points, while the Lifestyle variant is no better than the control, because measurable outcomes drive the premium purchase.

arguments.decision_rule: Pursue a differentiated proposition only if one treatment variant's reservation rate exceeds the control by at least 3 percentage points and that variant records at least 40 reservations; if both variants are within 3 points of, or below, the control, keep the current consumer offer. Lifestyle wins: prototype the differentiated offer around design/status and pilot it in two Technogym retail boutiques. Health wins: prototype around data-driven coaching and pilot it in two boutiques. Neither beats control: do not build a differentiated line, keep the current offer and investigate a lower-price/subscription model next.

justification.learned: Technogym already reaches individual buyers: 500,000 private homes plus 100,000 wellness centres (technogym-500k-homes); its Consumer segment grew +8% H1 then accelerated (technogym-consumer-headwind); Retail, Wholesale and Inside Sales all grew (technogym-channels). Independent evidence is cautious: Cycling Weekly wants a ~25% price cut and notes 'hefty monthly subscription bills' (technogym-cw-price-subs); 22 of 40 home-equipment search terms downtrend (technogym-ggr-search-down); Peloton's connected-fitness sales fell as gyms reopened (technogym-peloton-2021-gyms). Demand exists by the company's account, but no source shows demand for a further differentiated premium proposition.
justification.uncertain: Whether home users would pay for a differentiated proposition at all, and which mechanism drives it: T1 (status/design) rests only on a company design claim (technogym-home-design), and T2 (measurable health outcomes) is weakly evidenced by a review noting subscription cost rather than health motivation (technogym-cw-price-subs). The independent review's call for a ~25% price cut could mean price sensitivity dominates either premium framing, which would favour keeping the current offer.
justification.why_next: A deposit-based concept test separates T1 from T2 because each predicts a different framing wins (lifestyle vs health), and the control arm tests both against the current offer, so the result decides develop-vs-keep. If neither premium framing beats the control, the next step is to keep the current offer and investigate a lower-price/subscription model.

examples.question: It is mid-2013. Should FLIR Systems develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its uncooled thermal imaging cores? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt thermal imaging devices if they perceive them as a safety or utility product for home use, because they value the ability to detect heat signatures for fire detection, home maintenance, or outdoor activities.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt thermal imaging devices if they perceive them as a utility product for outdoor recreation and hunting, because they value the ability to detect heat signatures for tracking game, navigation, or safety.

arguments.name: Paid reservation A/B test: home-safety vs outdoor thermal camera bundles
arguments.method: Target customers: US adults aged 25-60 who own a home and also hunt or do outdoor recreation at least monthly, screened via a targeted online panel. Treatment: A landing page for 'FLIR Home Monitor' at $499: an uncooled-core thermal camera that attaches to a phone, plus a wall mount, continuous power, a high-temperature audible alarm, and an energy/water-leak audit guide, positioned as a home-safety/utility tool. Page template, price and deposit ask are identical to the control. Control: A landing page for 'FLIR Field Scout' at $499: the same uncooled-core thermal camera that attaches to a phone, plus weatherproof housing, 8-hour battery, handheld grip, rail mount and lanyard, positioned for spotting game and night navigation. Page template, price and deposit ask are identical to the treatment.
arguments.sample: Recruit 800 participants (400 per arm) over three weeks from a US online panel, screened for home ownership and monthly hunting/outdoor recreation, then randomized to one landing page.
arguments.measure: Share of participants who complete a $20 refundable deposit to reserve the $499 product within 14 days of seeing the page; deposits are refunded after the test.

prediction_by_theory.T1: The home-safety bundle has a deposit rate at least 3 percentage points higher than the outdoor bundle.
prediction_by_theory.T2: The outdoor bundle has a deposit rate at least 3 percentage points higher than the home-safety bundle.

arguments.decision_rule: The winning bundle must reach at least a 5% deposit rate, and beat the rival by at least 3 percentage points, to justify further investment. Below 5% or a margin under 3 points means no consumer launch now. If home-safety wins (at least 5% deposit rate and at least 3 points ahead), run a bounded 500-unit pilot with one home-improvement retail partner. If outdoor wins on the same criteria, run a bounded 500-unit pilot with one outdoor specialty retailer. If neither reaches 5% or the margin is under 3 points, do not expand to consumers now; continue the B2B/no-expansion route and re-test only if core cost falls or a partner shows demand evidence.

justification.learned: Pre-mid-2013 sources show FLIR had a low-cost prosumer camera, not a consumer line: the i3 launched Feb 2011 at US$1,195, "the most affordable high-quality infrared camera" for "every electrician and engineer" (flir-eb-i3price; flir-mb-toolbox). Prices had "decreased continuously" (flir-mb-pricefall). A 2007 report shows thermal imaging sold as a $150+ technician service, not a consumer purchase (flir-spk-service). No pre-mid-2013 source shows individual buyers purchasing for home safety or hunting, or a retail/DTC channel; demand and willingness to pay are unknown. 2014 sources excluded.
justification.uncertain: The open question is whether any consumer use case would produce enough real commitment to justify a consumer line, and which motivation is stronger: home safety/utility (T1) or outdoor/hunting (T2). No pre-2013 source shows consumer price elasticity at a $499-$1,195 price, repeat purchase, channel economics, or purchase frequency. Low core cost alone does not establish consumer pull.
justification.why_next: This paid-reservation test is worth the proposed €18,000/8-week cost because it can change the decision: it measures deposits, not stated interest, and separates T1 from T2 because the home bundle embodies continuous home monitoring while the outdoor bundle embodies field use, so each theory predicts the opposite bundle wins among dual-motivated homeowners who also recreate outdoors. The 5% minimum-demand and 3-point margin thresholds stop the project if neither use case clears the bar. Limitation: bundle features could drive the margin rather than pure motivation, so the winning result only funds a 500-unit pilot, not a full product line.
